claim: Selection of Acinetobacter baumannii in structured and unstructured environments containing ciprofloxacin produced distinct genotypes and phenotypes.
source: Previously, we showed that selection of the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii in both structured and unstructured environments containing the antibiotic ciprofloxacin produced distinct genotypes and phenotypes, with lower resistance in biofilms as well as collateral sensitivity to β-lactam drugs (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos-Lopez et al., 2019

claim: Selection of A. baumannii in biofilms resulted in lower resistance to ciprofloxacin compared to planktonic selection.
source: Previously, we showed that selection of the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii in both structured and unstructured environments containing the antibiotic ciprofloxacin produced distinct genotypes and phenotypes, with lower resistance in biofilms as well as collateral sensitivity to β-lactam drugs (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos-Lopez et al., 2019

claim: Selection of A. baumannii in biofilms resulted in collateral sensitivity to β-lactam drugs.
source: Previously, we showed that selection of the pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii in both structured and unstructured environments containing the antibiotic ciprofloxacin produced distinct genotypes and phenotypes, with lower resistance in biofilms as well as collateral sensitivity to β-lactam drugs (Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos-Lopez et al., 2019

claim: The effects of history were reduced by increasingly strong selection in new drugs.
source: The effects of history were reduced by increasingly strong selection in new drugs, but not erased, at times revealing important contingencies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing changes in variance contributions over time

claim: A history of selection in structured environments constrained resistance to new drugs.
source: A history of selection in structured environments constrained resistance to new drugs and led to frequent loss of resistance to the initial drug by genetic reversions and not compensatory mutations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing lower resistance evolution in biofilm-derived populations

claim: A history of selection in structured environments led to frequent loss of resistance to the initial drug by genetic reversions and not compensatory mutations.
source: A history of selection in structured environments constrained resistance to new drugs and led to frequent loss of resistance to the initial drug by genetic reversions and not compensatory mutations.
evidence: Supported by genomic sequencing data showing reversion mutations in adeL

claim: Despite strong selective pressures of antibiotics leading to genetic parallelism, history can etch potential vulnerabilities to orthogonal drugs.
source: This research demonstrates that despite strong selective pressures of antibiotics leading to genetic parallelism, history can etch potential vulnerabilities to orthogonal drugs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing collateral sensitivity patterns

claim: Evolution can be surprisingly repeatable when selection is strong even among distantly related lineages or in different environments.
source: A wealth of recent research has shown that evolution can be surprisingly repeatable when selection is strong even among distantly related lineages or in different environments (Lieberman et al., 2011; Lassig et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2018), but disparate outcomes become more likely as the footprint of history (i.e. differences in genetic background caused by chance and selection in different environments) increases (Blount et al., 2018; Benton et al., 2021; Mahrt et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Disparate evolutionary outcomes become more likely as the footprint of history increases.
source: A wealth of recent research has shown that evolution can be surprisingly repeatable when selection is strong even among distantly related lineages or in different environments (Lieberman et al., 2011; Lassig et al., 2017; Turner et al., 2018), but disparate outcomes become more likely as the footprint of history (i.e. differences in genetic background caused by chance and selection in different environments) increases (Blount et al., 2018; Benton et al., 2021; Mahrt et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: In the absence of chance and history, selection will cause the most fit genotype to fix in the particular environment.
source: In the absence of chance and history, selection will cause the most fit genotype to fix in the particular environment, and provided this variant is available, evolution will be perfectly predictable (Bailey et al., 2015; Lassig et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations and established evolutionary theory

claim: Historical and stochastic processes inevitably produce some degree of contingency, making evolution less predictable.
source: However, historical and stochastic processes inevitably produce some degree of contingency, making evolution less predictable, reflecting the importance of evolutionary history (Blount et al., 2008; Meyer et al., 2012; Bajić et al., 2018; Blount et al., 2018; Card et al., 2019; Galardini et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The evolution of a new trait is a stochastic process that depends on available genetic variation capable of producing a new trait.
source: The evolution of a new trait, whether by horizontally acquired genes or de novo mutation, is a stochastic process that depends on available genetic variation capable of producing a new trait (Khan et al., 2011; Salverda et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khan et al., 2011 and Salverda et al., 2011

claim: Antibiotics can impose strong selection pressure on microbial populations, leading to highly repeatable evolutionary outcomes.
source: Antibiotics can impose strong selection pressure on microbial populations, leading to highly repeatable evolutionary outcomes (Vogwill et al., 2014; Lukačišinová et al., 2020; Scribner et al., 2020), with the level of parallelism predicted to depend on the strength of antibiotic pressure (Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The level of parallelism in antibiotic resistance evolution is predicted to depend on the strength of antibiotic pressure.
source: Antibiotics can impose strong selection pressure on microbial populations, leading to highly repeatable evolutionary outcomes (Vogwill et al., 2014; Lukačišinová et al., 2020; Scribner et al., 2020), with the level of parallelism predicted to depend on the strength of antibiotic pressure (Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018

claim: Evolutionary history can alter the distribution of fitness effects of AMR mutations.
source: However, evolutionary history can also alter the distribution of fitness effects of AMR mutations, their mechanisms of action, or their degree of conferred resistance (Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007; Hall and MacLean, 2011; Yen and Papin, 2017; Barbosa et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: The phenotypic effect of any given mutation acquired is contingent on prior events.
source: The phenotypic effect of any given mutation acquired is contingent on prior events and will determine the potential of further adaptations to a given environment (Travisano et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Travisano et al., 1995

claim: The effects of a given mutation can vary in different genetic backgrounds (epistasis).
source: For example, the effects of a given mutation can vary in different genetic backgrounds (epistasis) or in different environments (pleiotropy) and those mutations can constrain further adaptations (Trindade et al., 2009; Hall and MacLean, 2011; Yen and Papin, 2017; Gifford et al., 2018; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies and established genetic knowledge

claim: The effects of a given mutation can vary in different environments (pleiotropy).
source: For example, the effects of a given mutation can vary in different genetic backgrounds (epistasis) or in different environments (pleiotropy) and those mutations can constrain further adaptations (Trindade et al., 2009; Hall and MacLean, 2011; Yen and Papin, 2017; Gifford et al., 2018; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies and established genetic knowledge

claim: Chance differences in the mutations acquired, their order of occurrence, or compensatory mutations can affect the eventual level of resistance.
source: Additionally, chance differences in the mutations acquired, their order of occurrence, or compensatory mutations that decrease resistance costs can affect the eventual level of resistance and its evolutionary success in the population (Salverda et al., 2011; Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Salverda et al., 2011 and Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018

claim: When large populations of 1 × 10^7 CFU/mL or higher are propagated, the probability that every base pair is mutated at least once approaches 99% after ~80 generations.
source: When large populations, 1 × 107 CFU/mL or higher, of bacteria are propagated, the probability that every base pair is mutated at least once approaches 99% after ~80 generations (Lynch et al., 2016; Santos-Lopez et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lynch et al., 2016 and Santos-Lopez et al., 2019

claim: Most mutations are initially rare and subject to genetic drift until they reach a critical frequency of establishment, when selection dominates their fate.
source: Yet chance still remains important because most mutations are initially rare and subject to genetic drift until they reach a critical frequency of establishment, when selection dominates their fate (Heffernan and Wahl, 2002; Good et al., 2017; Cooper, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies and established population genetics theory

claim: The success of new mutations will be determined by their survival of drift, the chance that they co-occur with other fit mutants, and by their relative fitness.
source: Thus, the success of new mutations will be determined by their survival of drift, the chance that they co-occur with other fit mutants, and by their relative fitness, which is shaped by selection and history (Nguyen Ba et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nguyen Ba et al., 2019 and inference from population genetics principles

claim: Acinetobacter baumannii is a leading agent of multidrug-resistant infections worldwide.
source: Here we use this framework to measure the relative roles of history, chance, and selection in the evolution of AMR phenotypes and genotypes in the ESKAPE (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii, a leading agent of multidrug-resistant infections worldwide and named as an urgent threat by the CDC (CDC, 2019).

claim: Acinetobacter baumannii is named as an urgent threat by the CDC.

evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: After 3 days of growth in subinhibitory concentrations of CAZ, chance explained 7.6% of variation in resistance phenotypes.

claim: By day 12 of CAZ treatment, selection explained 47.8% of variation in resistance phenotypes.

claim: By day 12 of CAZ treatment, history explained 31.4% of variation in resistance phenotypes.

claim: Strong selective pressures can diminish or erase the effects of history.

claim: The level of evolved resistance converges and may be predictable.

claim: Strong antibiotic selection has the potential to overcome but do not entirely eliminate historical differences in resistance.
source: Strong antibiotic selection has the potential to overcome but do not entirely eliminate historical differences in resistance.

claim: B populations became significantly more sensitive to CIP after CAZ selection, but P populations did not.

claim: The emergence of collateral sensitivity may depend on prior selection in different environments.

evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: For IMI resistance after CAZ selection, selection explained 44.3% of the variation, history contributed 23.0%, and chance 32.2%.
source: As expected, all 12 populations evolved in CAZ became more resistant to IMI (two-tailed nested t-test p<0.0001, t = 7.507, df = 34), and selection was the most important force (p<0.05), explaining almost 44.3% of the variation, while history contributed 23.0% and chance 32.2% (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: No overall change in resistance occurred following 3 days in subinhibitory concentrations of IMI.
